lesson.title: Circuits as Black Boxes: Two-Port Networks
lesson.summary: A two-port network characterizes a circuit purely by how voltage and current at an input port and an output port relate to each other, with input and output resistance as two of its four defining parameters.
lesson.body:
So far, every technique in this chapter has treated a circuit as one interconnected whole and solved for every voltage and current inside it. A two port network takes a different view: it treats a circuit as a black box with exactly two pairs of accessible terminals, an input port and an output port, and asks only how voltages and currents at those two ports relate to each other, ignoring whatever complexity is hidden inside. This viewpoint is what lets engineers characterize an amplifier, a filter, or a transmission line with a small table of numbers instead of a full internal schematic.

The most direct way to characterize a two port network is with z parameters, which express both port voltages as linear combinations of both port currents: V1 equals z11 times I1, plus z12 times I2, and V2 equals z21 times I1, plus z22 times I2. Two of these four numbers are already familiar under other names. Input resistance is exactly z11, the ratio of V1 to I1 measured with the output port left open, meaning I2 equals zero. Output resistance is exactly z22, the ratio of V2 to I2 measured with the input port left open, meaning I1 equals zero. The two cross terms, z12 and z21, capture how each port influences the other, information that input resistance and output resistance alone cannot provide.

Consider a T shaped resistive network: a 2 ohm resistor, R1, in series from the input terminal to a middle node, a 3 ohm resistor, R2, in series from that same middle node to the output terminal, and a 5 ohm resistor, R3, from the middle node down to the common ground rail shared by both ports. To find z11, leave the output open, so I2 equals zero, which forces the current through R2 to be zero as well, since it has nowhere to go. All of I1 then flows through R1 and R3 in series, so z11 equals R1 plus R3, which is 2 plus 5, or 7 ohms. Since no current flows through R2, there is no drop across it, so V2 simply equals the voltage across R3, which is I1 times R3, giving z21 equals R3, or 5 ohms.

By the same reasoning with the ports swapped, leaving the input open so I1 equals zero, z22 equals R2 plus R3, which is 3 plus 5, or 8 ohms, and z12 equals R3, or 5 ohms again, matching z21 exactly, a symmetry that holds for any network built entirely from resistors. So this network's full z parameter description is z11 equals 7 ohms, z12 equals z21 equals 5 ohms, and z22 equals 8 ohms, a compact four number summary that lets anyone predict the port behavior of this network without ever seeing the internal T structure.

Z parameters are only one of several equivalent ways to describe a two port network. Y parameters express port currents in terms of port voltages instead, h parameters mix one voltage and one current on each side, a combination that happens to match how transistors are usually measured, and every one of these parameter sets can be converted into any other by straightforward algebra, since they all describe the same underlying physical relationships. What never changes across any of these forms is that input resistance and output resistance are always the two easiest numbers to extract, since each one comes from a single measurement with the opposite port simply left open, which is exactly why they are singled out as prerequisites for understanding the full two port picture.
